Gaming_Tech.title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.

The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.

Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global.

"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."

Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.

Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."

Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.

Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice.

"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."

If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

Gaming_Tech.title: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
Gaming_Tech.text:
German police have detained a Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang which caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death.

The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death.

The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates.

Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime.

The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K.

He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday.

According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country.

He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims.

Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency.

While his extradition was first reported in early October, external, the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations.

Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab.

A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere.

King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly".

A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result".

"The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time.

A similar attack in 2020 by a different hacker group on a hospital in Düsseldorf in Germany led to a negligent homicide investigation being opened after an elderly patient died.

It was later dropped after medical experts concluded the patient's condition was so severe that they would have died regardless of the issues caused by the cyber-attack.

Prosecutors could also not definitively prove that it was the direct cause of death.

In total, the Synnovis hack in 2024 disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption.

The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom.

Gaming_Tech.title: Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram grooming becoming 'quicker and easier'
Gaming_Tech.text:
Experts are urging parents to talk to their children amid warnings social media grooming is becoming "quicker" and "easier" than ever before.

Childline said Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram were the top platforms children named in counselling about online sexual abuse last year. The companies have been approached for comment.

Avon and Somerset Police's child exploitation prevention officer Andri Nicolau said children as young as five can be targeted through social media, gaming and messaging platforms. She urged parents to encourage kids to ask for help without fear of blame or punishment.

The warning comes after three men were jailed for grooming a 17-year-old girl on Snapchat before raping her.

Research by the NSPCC found sexual communication offences involving children in the South West have more than doubled since the offence was introduced seven years ago, to 756 in 2024/25.

Of those, 300 were recorded by Avon and Somerset Police, 96 by Gloucestershire Constabulary and 61 by Wiltshire Police.

The charity also said Snapchat was mentioned in 324 counselling sessions about online sexual abuse between April 2025 and March 2026, a 19% increase on the previous year.

TikTok (234) and Instagram (197) were the next most frequently mentioned platforms.

Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, said: "It's deeply disturbing that hundreds of children have come to us in the past year alone, disclosing experiences of online sexual abuse linked to these popular apps and platforms.

"These crimes are highly distressing for victims, often leaving children and their families to deal with devastating lifelong impacts."

Another recent example involved Suleman Aqeel, from Speedwell in Bristol, who was jailed for 17 years at Bristol Crown Court on 30 September.

Aqeel used social media, including Snapchat, to arrange to meet young girls. He also filmed some of his offences and threatened to share intimate videos and images.

New data suggests that this particular form of exploitation of children, known as 'sextortion', has also reached record levels.

The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) said there has been a sharp rise in the number of young people contacting its confidential Report Remove helpline, external because they fear sexual images of themselves have been shared, or could be shared, online.

Criminals try to extort or blackmail their victims by threatening to publish the images, which have often been taken by the child themselves.

Nicolau said children spending more time online meant they were increasingly vulnerable to grooming, which is "easier" and "quicker" than ever before.

"With online gaming and social media, you have kids from five years old online, some of them have their own phones, so it can be any age," she said.

She works with schools to inform children how to be safe online, but said they are often unaware of the risks, including not viewing people they meet online as strangers and expecting them to be "nasty" from the start.

Nicolau encouraged any child or young person who believes they are being groomed to "find someone they are comfortable with and speak to them".

She said the police might not be the first choice, but speaking to somebody they trust is what mattered.

Nicolau urged parents to talk to their children and not take away devices or ban them from platforms, warning this could make them feel they were to blame.

"Sit down with your child, tell them it's not their fault, even if they've sent indecent images of themselves," she said.

"Believe them and give them the authorisation to say whatever they need to say."

Ella Bradshaw, the NSPCC's policy and public affairs officer, advised parents to start conversations about online safety as early as possible so that children know that they have a "safe adult" to go to.

"Often, particularly if it's to do with grooming or any kind of sexual or romantic relationship, children can be really scared of being judged and embarrassed to talk," said Bradshaw.

"Making sure that your child knows that you will stand by them, that you will respond with warmth and care rather than judging them or blaming them for what's going on is really important."

James Simmons-Read, who leads the Children's Society national exploitation prevention programme, said there are "huge concerns" about the growing scale of child sexual abuse and exploitation online.

"Perpetrators are always adapting ways they can better reach young people, whether that's through gaming or social media," he said.

He said another worrying trend was young people turning to AI rather than adults for advice and support about online harms.

Simmons-Read urged parents to normalise conversations with young people about their online lives.

Simmons-Read said the social media ban for under 16s, which is due to come into force in 2027, "doesn't go far enough", could be bypassed by criminals and could even discourage young people from speaking up about online grooming.

"We want tech platforms to invest more in detecting exploitation when it's happening on their platforms," he said.

A government spokesperson said it was preparing legislation to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images on their devices, which would make the UK the first country to do so.

"Alongside this, tech companies must be part of the solution and meet their legal and moral obligations. Where they fall short, the government will not hesitate to step in," the spokesperson said.

Kerry Smith, chief executive of the IWF, said: "We welcome the commitment to introducing nudity blocking technology on children's devices – but there really is no time to lose."

Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, said it is working to "fight and prevent grooming in a range of ways".

A Meta spokesperson said: "This includes restricting contact between adults and teens they're not connected to, and using technology to find and remove known child exploitation imagery.

"We also use behavioural signals to identify accounts showing possible signs of grooming or a sexual interest in children.

"Based on the strength of the signals, we either prevent them from finding and following teens or we remove their account completely."

Snapchat and TikTok have all been approached by the BBC for comment.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Gaming_Tech.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
Gaming_Tech.text:
Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.

From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16 in England and Wales.

The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.

Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".

She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable".

Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.

It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences".

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, Baroness Bertin said porn showing strangulation had "absolutely sort of normalised this kind of sexual violence".

"That has to come to an end and I hope this law change will be the beginning of that," she said - adding that it aimed to "marry up" differences in the law about what was acceptable online and offline.

Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent, but its depiction online is currently not illegal.

Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales.

Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences".

But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said.

"If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added.

"It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal."

Gaming_Tech.title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
Gaming_Tech.text:
Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.

For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.

"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.

While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".

Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.

The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.

Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."

The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.

Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.

When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.

In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.

Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.

This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.

"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.

The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.

Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.

But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.

Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.

Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.

In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.

A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.

"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."

The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.

The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.

This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"

Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.

Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.

Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.

Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."

The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.

Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

Gaming_Tech.title: World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countries
Gaming_Tech.text:
The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence.

While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs.

Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose.

“We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said.

“Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.”

Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language.

“There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.”

He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector.

The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand.

Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed.

She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work.

“If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.”

The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection.

Georgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers.

“When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.”

Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work.

Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets.

“We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report finds
Gaming_Tech.text:
In December 2025, Morgan Dorfman received distressing news: a student at her daughter’s Pennsylvania high school was making AI-generated pornographic material using the daughter’s image.

He was using an artificial intelligence image-editing app called Movely to create sexual videos from pictures of her daughter and five other girls.

What Dorfman’s daughter experienced is not an anomaly: students in high schools across the US are reporting similar cases. Their classmates are generating nonconsensual pornographic or nude imagery using so-called “nudify apps”.

Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores, and most US states have implemented laws that criminalize possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material.

However, in spite of regulations prohibiting them, nudification apps are still proliferating and remain accessible to teens, according to a report from the digital advocacy group Tech Transparency Project (TTP) shared exclusively with the Guardian and released on Monday.

TTP researchers created four test accounts, two Apple accounts and two Google accounts, indicating the account holders were 13 years old. They searched for image-editing or face-swapping apps using terms such as “AI video generator” or “adult AI”. Using these accounts for a purported 13-year-old, the researchers were able to download 135 apps with features enabling them to strip people of their clothes or swap their faces on to nude bodies. The researchers disrobed women in AI-generated images in their tests rather than using photographs of real women.

At the time of her daughter’s distress, Dorfman didn’t know it was possible to create pornographic material of an everyday person so easily.

“All the girls were very scared and confused about what to do next,” Dorfman said. “I knew what a deepfake was, but I thought it was like Taylor Swift and people using celebrities’ [images],” Dorfman said. “I didn’t know it was possible to take any picture or any screenshot of anybody that you have and do this.”

Dorfman, a mother of four, spent weeks trying to figure out how the app worked and compiling material to educate other parents. She downloaded Movely and was immediately prompted to create suggestive videos using any image. The free version promoted sexually suggestive templates including “clothes explosion”, “brassiere unfasten” and “underwear drop”, according to a demonstration Dorfman put together for parents that the Guardian reviewed. In the paid version, it became more explicit: she saw templates for the types of pornographic situations in which, according a classmate, her daughter had appeared.

Both Apple and Google prohibit these types of apps from being distributed on their platforms. The companies also will often age-gate apps with adult content, restricting or blocking minors’ access. However, TPP researchers found that the companies largely rely on the developers to determine whether their apps are appropriate for certain ages.

“Many nudify apps identified in the investigation were inaccurately rated as suitable for minors – meaning the teen users could access them even when parental controls were activated,” the report said.

Researchers found that one face-swapping app, which was advertised to them with an image of a woman performing oral sex, was rated appropriate for ages four and up. The free version of the app prompted users to superimpose real women’s faces on to templates of women in lingerie or, if users paid, in pornographic situations. The researchers were able to buy a subscription to the app from a 13-year-old’s account without an alert to a linked parental account.

Google said the company regularly takes “proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content”.

“When violations are detected or reported to us, we investigate and take swift action, which in this case included suspending violating apps and restricting related search terms on our store,” a Google spokesperson, Dan Jackson, said in a statement.

After TTP contacted Apple seeking comment on the findings of their study, Apple implemented changes that strengthened content moderation guidelines. The company now requires developers to pre-emptively prevent and remove nonconsensual intimate imagery including AI-generated images. Apple also said that the company reviews every app before it is published and that if a developer misrepresents any features, the company removes the app and its developers. The company said in addition to apps they already removed before the TTP report was shared with them, the company has also “taken action” on the remaining apps mentioned in the report.

“A number of the apps in this report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities,” said an Apple spokesperson, Adam Dema. “We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process – a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch.”

Of the four accounts the researchers created, two were placed under parental controls that only allowed users to download apps marked suitable for 13-year-olds and only then with a parental signoff. However, the researchers found that neither Apple nor Google required or suggested parental signoff to acquire any of the nudification apps.

One app, Image to Video Maker-Vidou AI, was rated appropriate for users aged nine and older. Upon opening the app, users were greeted by an image of a topless woman on a bus, according to the TTP study.

“The app had a feature that promised to digitally undress any person – and to demonstrate, it showed nude images of female celebrities,” the report read.

Age restrictions were also not entirely effective, the study found. In one case, when the researchers tried to download an adult-rated app from the Apple App Store, they came across a pop-up warning that the app contained “age-restricted material”. But all they had to do was confirm they were 17 or older, which Apple allowed the account to do despite its registered age being 13. The Google account without parental controls was blocked three times from downloading an age-restricted app but otherwise allowed the researchers to download nudification apps that were self-reported to be age-appropriate.

The Apple account that TTP set up parental controls for was still able to find and download 24 so-called “nudify” apps because they were all rated as appropriate for 13-year-olds. The Google account with parental controls was able to download 51 of these apps.

Removing image and video editing platforms from app stores was also not enough to prevent its use. In the course of TTP’s research, Apple took down 25 of the nudify apps, and Google took down six. However, the researchers were able to continue using the app since they had already downloaded it.

Dorfman had a similar experience with Movely, she said. While preparing a presentation for parents and law enforcement officials, she returned to the app and App Store to take screenshots when she realized it was no longer available to download. However, the app was already on her phone and it remained entirely functional. She was also still being charged for her paid subscription.

Once these nonconsensual images and videos are created, accountability proves evasive, Dorfman has found. “I just wanted someone to make him delete all of these videos,” she said.

In her daughter’s case, Dorfman feels her school has downplayed what happened. In a school-wide email the Guardian reviewed, the principal wrote that her daughter’s classmate did use the app to animate images of other students but that there was no evidence he had done anything inappropriate.

However, days later, Radnor police criminally charged him with harassment.

“The whole thing was dismissed as ‘it’s not real,’” Dorfman said. “The haunting trauma as a mom is that I can’t tell [my daughter] those videos are gone or who had them. We can’t search everyone’s phones, and he deleted the app.”

Gaming_Tech.title: ‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshoots
Gaming_Tech.text:
Stand in any vaguely photogenic spot these days on holiday and the chances are you will come across people posing with raised phones and even ring lights. Some may be influencers with huge audiences on social media, others just overkeen Instagram users. With hotels and beauty spots now so overrun, however, bans on photography are coming into place.

The five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, known for its glamorous clientele, views of the Côte d’Azur and a stunning infinity pool, has brought in rules against photoshoots: no longer allowed without prior permission.

According to reports, this has been prompted by people booking lunch reservations and bringing bags of clothing and jewellery. Instead of sitting down to eat, they have used their time at the hotel for photoshoots of themselves in different outfits, creating images to post to their social media accounts.

Less glamorous spots are also clamping down. The Hollies, a Cheshire farm shop which has become a popular content stop thanks to the Love Island star Molly-Mae Hague posting images from there, has banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm.

Meanwhile Jeremy King, the London restaurateur behind places such as Simpson’s in the Strand and the Park, wrote an article in the Evening Standard earlier this year titled: “I’m fed up with influencers over-running my restaurant – enough is enough.”

In the US, a shop on Nantucket, an island off Cape Cod, Massachusetts, went viral earlier this year for a sign reading “no influencers”, while the town of Pomfret in Vermont has banned influencers taking pictures in front of foliage in autumn. In Fujikawaguchiko in Japan, a screen has been put up near a convenience store to stop people taking pictures there in front of Mount Fuji.

Part of the argument from venues is that these photoshoots jeopardise privacy and discretion, especially as expected at expensive hotels. Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc’s manager, Sophie Volant, told Travel Weekly: “As much as [guests] appreciate having people in the restaurants and in the bars, they also want their summer home to remain private. We had to think about a solution.”

Anna Fedou, the chief marketing officer at the Beaumier hotel group, says it sometimes works with influencers to capture content to promote its luxury hotels, which include Les Roches Rouges near Marseille, loved for its photogenic pool. The group does not have specific rules around photography, Fedou says, but stays mindful of its primary purpose.

“We’re in the business of hospitality, not running photo studios,” she says. “People travel from all over the world to experience the atmosphere, sense of space and feeling that make a hotel unique. It’s our responsibility to protect that.”

Rules around photography at hotels and restaurants mirror a trend away from capturing the moment and towards being in it. Alex Goat, the founder of the youth culture agency Livity, compares these rules to clubs asking visitors to put stickers over their phones’ cameras. “They want to signify that they’re here for people who love music. There’s something potentially similar [here],” she says. “It’s ‘I’m here because I want to enjoy the space’ rather than ‘I’m here to document something to other people’.”

Part of the disapproval towards influencers is a common misconception is that they are paid well for such content. Sometimes, as with Beaumier hotels, influencers will produce posts in exchange for a free room, but the idea is that brands will want to make deals with influencers due to their association with glamorous locations. “The majority are creating most of their content for their audiences for free,” explains Nicole Ocran, an influencer who set up the Creator Union to represent those in the industry. “They create content in the hope of courting brands and seeing who will bite.”

There has been previous outrage around influencers’ behaviour, as in 2021 when Love Island stars travelled to Dubai during lockdown, for example. And if there is an underlying snobbery to a luxury hotel instigating anti-photoshoot policies, there may be sexism, too. “Influencer culture has always been vilified in popular culture,” says Sophie Bishop, the author of Influencer Creep. “It’s a very feminised form of media, that’s bound up in promotional culture.”

Ocran agrees. “Most people have a particular stereotype in mind,” she says. “That isn’t to say that influencers and content creators can’t overstep or be insufferable when getting their shots and filming in public.”

Fedou believes that the key is to walk a balance that engages with social media content while keeping a restful experience at hotels. “Influencers will generally choose quieter moments for shooting content, to capture the space without disturbing others,” she says. “Les Roches Rouges has a relaxed atmosphere, but guest experience always comes first.”

While the backlash might be aimed at influencers with lots of followers, over 5.4 billion people use social media every day.

Ocran hopes that rules around photography might promote a more balanced attitude to social media in general. “[It’s] pushing back against the idea that not every space is meant for public consumption, and not every experience should be turned into content,” she says. “And as a creator, that’s quite a healthy message to send to us all.”

Entertainment.title: Christiane Amanpour: CNN reporter and anchor to leave network after 43 years
Entertainment.text:
CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the organisation next year after more than four decades.

"After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said in a statement., external

The 68-year-old said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral".

CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her "before she departs next year".

Amanpour began working for CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk, and went on to become one of the network's best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars.

She has presented her own nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.

In a memo to staff on Monday, Thompson wrote: "Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months.

"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.

"In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship," he added.

In her own statement, Amanpour said she wanted to thank "all the amazingly talented people I've worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews."

Amanpour reflected on her "very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between".

"It's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she continued, "as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favour."

Entertainment.title: Selena Gomez says vaping has affected her voice
Entertainment.text:
Selena Gomez has said vaping nicotine has changed the way her voice sounds.

"I'm not gonna be able to change my voice," the singer, 34, said in a candid Instagram post, external on Sunday. "I vaped nicotine a lot."

"Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you're going through it, or if you're even trying to vape, it's just not worth it," she continued.

"It's so stupid and it changed my voice," she reiterated, then laughed: "So if you guys don't like listening to my voice, that's totally understandable. I don't mind. Just don't listen to it."

The singer and actress, who has the chronic autoimmune disease lupus, has previously suggested that the condition was affecting her vocal cords.

Asked about her voice in an Instagram Q&A last December,, external she said: "Sometimes things happen. I get weird. My throat kind of swells inside sometimes. That's all."⁠

Lupus flare-ups can cause inflammation around the larynx (voice box), which can cause your voice to become raspy and strained - similar to the symptoms of a cold.

Gomez's voice has also deepened with age, which is not uncommon. However, some fans have fixated on the change, posting compilation videos showing the evolution of her speaking style, external on YouTube.

In her Instagram video, the Only Murders In The Building star noted she had recently weaned herself off nicotine.

"I am really excited because I stopped and I just hope I can keep it up," she said.

"It's really hard, but I know if you are going through something you can get through it too. It sucks."

Entertainment.title: Kylie Jenner makes Victoria Secret debut in $50 million bra
Entertainment.text:
Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra.

The make-up mogul surprised the crowd at the lingerie giant's annual show on Sunday while wearing the famed Fantasy Bra, which was made of 18-carat gold and 4,410 diamonds, according to the designer.

The Fantasy Bra has been a key feature of the show over the years and wearing it is typically seen as an honour and defining moment for the chosen model.

The Kardashians star, 29, being selected to wear the piece delighted some fans, while many others criticised the brand for not giving the opportunity to a veteran supermodel.

Social media and marketing expert Joel Marlinarson says the moment was well-engineered and generated "a lot of conversation" on what it means for the "future of modelling and social media".

"Of course Kylie represents a new era of celebrity where brands are prioritising who's going to bring the most eyeballs, as opposed to who fits the cookie cutter definition of a model," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

Marlinarson says young viewers have a connection with Jenner having grown up watching her on social media and through her reality show with her Kardashian sisters.

However, he says there will be a section of the audience who remembers "the iconic Naomi Campbell era of fashion" who might see Jenner being given this moment as a "betrayal of what they know".

"Ultimately, this represents this new era of marketing where brands, particularly Victoria's Secret and legacy brands, they don't want to take risks," he says.

"They want to bring in somebody who they know is going to generate eyeballs, who's going to generate those headlines and who can consistently raise a crowd and that's exactly what Victoria's Secret has done."

Some fans cheered on Jenner in the comments of a video shared on Victoria's Secret Instagram page unveiling the dramatic look., external

While many others branded it as "pure disrespect to real models" and questioned why she was picked out of a "room full of talented models".

One said the show has "gone from iconic glamour to an influencer circus" and they felt "social media clout and performative inclusivity have replaced real modeling talent, elegance, and runway presence".

Chief creative officer at Victoria's Secret, Adam Selman, told Vogue, external that Jenner was picked for being a "cultural powerhouse".

"Kylie really extends beyond fashion, beyond culture, beyond TV, beyond one singular thing," he adds.

"That's the exact same thing that we do.

"Like, the show is so big, it's true entertainment, and I think that she is a great catalyst for that."

Entertainment.title: You Can See Everything: Elizabeth Holmes documentary stuns with huge box office debut
Entertainment.text:
A three-hour documentary on the tech fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has raked in a whopping $15 million (£11.25m) on its box office debut, despite a limited run at 855 screens across the US and Canada.

The eagerly anticipated film, You Can See Everything, finds Holmes letting filmmakers into her California home in 2023, during the month before she began an 11-year prison sentence.

It was co-directed by comedian Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim who find themselves embroiled in the story, growing suspicious that Holmes and her partner are withholding information.

US publication Deadline noted the film had enjoyed "easily the second best opening ever for a [non-music] documentary at the box office", after Michael Moore's 2004 film about the US's invasion of Iraq, Fahrenheit 9/11.

Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors in her medical testing company Theranos, fuelling a media circus that has been chronicled in books, podcasts and the mini-series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

In You Can See Everything, Canadian comedian Fielder - known for his awkward, deadpan and at-times surreal humour, on shows including The Rehearsal and The Curse - places himself inside the action, once again blurring the lines between documentary, social experiment and prank show.

We see notorious Silicon Valley founder Holmes and her partner Billy Evans invite a sceptical film crew to document her every move, 34 days before she's sent to prison.

Seyfried appears in the hybrid documentary to re-enact events and scenes that the documentary crew could not film or needed to reconstruct.

The first teaser trailer, external dropped last month, right after the film's surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado.

It went viral and launched many online memes of Holmes unblinkingly asking first-time filmmaker, Fielder: "Why would I deceive you?"

Entertainment.title: Emma Freud says Beatles' songs to star in Yesterday musical
Entertainment.text:
Film producer Emma Freud has confirmed The Beatles have agreed for their songs to feature in a stage version of the movie, Yesterday.

Freud is working on the show with her husband, Richard Curtis. They were behind the 2019 film and other box office hits, including Love Actually and Bridget Jones's Diary.

She called it "a huge deal", saying: "They've [The Beatles] never done that with a West End musical before. So it's the first time that you can kind of legally see The Beatles' music on stage, which is amazing."

Freud spoke to BBC Radio Suffolk on Monday, after she received an honorary doctorate for her work in film and broadcasting at the University of Suffolk on Saturday.

She said a theatre where the stage show will be performed had been chosen - "but I can't tell you what it is because I will get killed".

She confirmed the stage version of Yesterday would also be directed by Oscar-winner Danny Boyle, who oversaw the movie.

Freud said: "We're at workshop stages, so we've already had two workshops and we've got a third one coming up this month, where you sort of ask actors to come into a room and just interrogate the script and the songs and the staging, and see how it's going to work.

"Currently we're on the 11th draft of the script, because it isn't just taking a movie script and putting it on to a stage.

"It's the same story, but actually every beat of it becomes different, becomes theatrical rather than filmic.

"So it's been an incredible process to be a part of. I don't feel like I've ever done anything as big in my entire life."

On receiving her doctorate from the University of Suffolk, Freud said "the honour" was "so massive", because "Suffolk is my home and it's where I was brought up, and it's where my family has lived for generations".

Her family arrived in the county as Jewish refugees from Germany in the 1930s, escaping the tyranny of the Nazis.

Freud's work has also involved tackling poverty and inequality, and has included working as a creative director and executive producer at Comic Relief, external.

Entertainment.title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' after death of son Presley at 27
Entertainment.text:
Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber.

"He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," she posted on Instagram, next to a black-and-white photo of him. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability."

The 27-year-old died on 20 September at a rehab facility in California. Police said officials are investigating his death as a suspected overdose.

Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.

Crawford wrote in the post on Sunday: "We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years."

"We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain," she also posted.

"Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia," she wrote in closing, with an emoji of angel wings.

The tribute also listed the dates of his birth and death.

The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner lists Gerber's case as pending additional investigation. The Santa Monica Police Department has said there is no indication foul play was involved in his death.

Gerber's sister Kaia also dedicated a post to him on Sunday which included a video of the two siblings as children dancing together, a photo of them standing near the ocean, and a four-page letter to "prez" typed out on a blue background.

In the letter, she said she had been scared of getting her ears pierced, so "you went first".

"But when I held the earring they took from your body, all I could think was: That belongs to you," she wrote.

"I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you," she also wrote. "How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in," she wrote.

In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use and frequently posted videos on Instagram himself for what he called "Mental Health Mondays".

His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.

If you're affected by any of the issues in this article you can find details of organisations who can help via the BBC Action Line.

Entertainment.title: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley Arena in one turbulent year
Entertainment.text:
When I first meet Turkish girl group manifest, we're on a boat cruising down the River Thames.

The six band members are clutching union jack umbrellas as they pose for press photographs and mingle with British pop acts, including K-pop-trained boyband dearALICE.

Netflix cameras are filming the evening for a six-part documentary. The group are in London hoping to build on their success in Turkey and reach an international audience.

Their ambitions come after a turbulent year at home, during which the band were prosecuted for public indecency over their outfits and dance moves during a concert in Istanbul.

A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the following night.

As the staging - complete with giant LED screens and the group's logo - is set up around them, the six members rehearse synchronised choreography alongside their back-up dancers.

The group consists of main vocalist Sueda Uluca, lead vocalist Lidya Pınar, sub-vocalist Mina Solak, sub-vocalist and main rapper Zeynep Sude Oktay, lead dancer Hilal Yelekçi and main dancer Esin Bahat.

But Wembley is just the beginning of their ambitions.

"After Wembley, we'll manifest Coachella and other big stages," says Hilal Yelekçi, playing on the group's name.

manifest were formed in February last year through the Turkish reality TV talent competition Big5 Türkiye, which saw contestants compete over several months for a place in the group.

They were mentored by established Turkish pop stars, including Gülçin Ergül, a former member of girl group Hepsi, who was also a judge on the show.

The band's rise has been rapid, and they now have more than six million monthly listeners on Spotify.

While in London, they released their first English-language single, TRALALA, which topped YouTube's daily music video chart on its release, ahead of videos from Shakira and Taylor Swift.

The music video was also their first to be filmed outside Turkey, with the group working with a largely British production crew in east London.

"Getting out from that safe zone was a bit stressful for us," says Pınar.

Despite their hopes to perform on British and American stages, they're keen to retain their Turkish identity.

"We want to reach a global audience with our Turkish songs actually, not with English ones," says Sude Oktay.

"We want to teach people to sing in Turkish."

Alongside Turkish girl group Hepsi, manifest cite the Spice Girls among their musical inspirations.

Pınar says her favourite Spice Girl is Baby Spice.

"Because of the pink. I'm pink and blonde, so it's obvious," she laughs.

They have also had the chance to meet one of the world's biggest pop stars, Dua Lipa.

The British-Albanian singer met manifest backstage before watching them perform at her Sunny Hill Festival in Kosovo in July this year.

"She came to our backstage and said a lot of great things," one member recalls.

"We really love her, her songs, her stage presence."

However, the band's road to success was threatened last year.

The trip to London comes just over a year after Turkish prosecutors launched an investigation into the group over allegations of violating public decency, following criticism of their outfits and choreography at an over-18s concert in Istanbul.

A Turkish court later ruled that their choreography and physical contact on stage amounted to exhibitionism.

In a post on X, Turkish politician Oktay Saral called for action so the group "can never repeat such acts".

The case also prompted criticism over artistic freedom in Turkey, where authorities have previously cancelled concerts and festivals over concerns about public morality.

Turkish singer Ceylan Ertem described the investigation as "an open attack on women's freedom and the performing arts".

The six members were handed suspended prison sentences of three months and 22 days. A ban preventing them from leaving Turkey was also lifted by the court.

Speaking to me in London, the group would not talk about the sentencing. Instead they spoke about wanting to inspire a new generation of Turkish girls.

"We are six different women, we have different hobbies... " says lead vocalist Pınar.

"We really, really want to see that little girls look at us and maybe they want to sing too, they want to dance too.

"Maybe they can get the power from us."

About 300 fans attended a signing event at a Turkish restaurant in London, giving the group their first chance to meet some of their UK-based supporters in person.

"Our concerts and events have been in Turkey before and we never met them face-to-face," says Pınar.

"It was a really cute moment for us."

On the day of the concert, there was a sense of excitement outside Wembley Arena as fans wearing manifest-branded headbands and carrying banners gathered.

The crowd was predominantly Turkish women in their 20s and 30s, many dressed in colours associated with the group.

Among them were friends Elif, 31, and Zeynep, 25, both Turkish women living in London, who reflected on the band's past year.

"I don't think I've ever heard of a girl band performing there," says Zeynep.

"I think I was seven when Hepsi were last together. It's maybe a once-in-a-lifetime experience."

Turkish pop star Tarkan previously performed at Wembley Arena in 2008.

For Elif, the concert has a wider significance.

"We are going through difficult times back home. It means girl power and empowerment, and just having fun and being together," she says.

"I feel like back home people came together to support them and criticise the treatment that they were receiving from the government."

Zeynep adds: "It's great to see them here, but I hope one day they will be back in Turkey and they'll be able to do whatever they want without getting persecuted for it."

The sense of girl power was strong as the group took to the Wembley stage, opening their set with Hileli before launching into TRALALA.

Throughout the evening the group switched between English and Turkish, at one point asking the audience who was Turkish and who was English. The loudest cheers came from the Turkish fans.

Alongside their own songs, they performed covers of One Direction's Story of My Life, the Spice Girls' Wannabe and the Pussycat Dolls' Hush Hush.

Hush Hush interpolates Gloria Gaynor's I Will Survive, which the group sang in Turkish, a striking moment for a group determined to bring their language to an international audience.

Even though manifest have their sights set on stages around the world, after several weeks in London they were missing some of the comforts of home.

"Turkish food, like kebab," says rapper Sude Oktay, before adding mantı, a traditional Turkish dumpling dish.

"Turkey is our home," says Pınar. "We miss our home."

Entertainment.title: Black Church Bay star Tom Cullen says LGBTQ representation 'really matters'
Entertainment.text:
Tom Cullen says he does not take the privilege of playing a gay character lightly.

Speaking at the screening of mystery-thriller Black Church Bay at the Iris Prize Festival, the Downton Abbey and House of the Dragon actor said representation mattered.

In the film, Cullen, from Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, plays a closeted man who finds he will go to any lengths to keep up appearances in his insular community.

It is not the first time Cullen has played a gay character, taking on his first ever role in 2011 British romantic drama Weekend.

He said: "What is wonderful is I feel like people can often pigeonhole queer cinema, and those two films show the spectrum and diversity that can be found."

The Cardiff-based Iris Prize LGBTQ+ Film Festival celebrates stories from across the world.

The annual festival, which works in partnership with BAFTA Cymru, is a seven-day event and this year celebrated its 20th anniversary.

Cullen said he approached the role of Barry "exactly the same" as he would a straight character.

"They are characters that you have to empathise with and understand. And fundamentally my job is empathy," he said.

"I remember doing Weekend and a big part of my research was interviewing and talking to my gay friends, talking about their experiences and trying to fully understand - but that's just research, which you should do for any character."

The 41-year-old said the script was "really challenging" and that was why he went for the role.

"The script was extraordinary and something that isn't usually made in the UK," he said. "It's so dark."

Black Church Bay was filmed in Anglesey and written and directed by Welsh-Irish filmmaker Rhys Marc Jones, who said he was inspired by the "real locations".

"The whole film was written with those locations in mind. I always wanted my debut film in Wales," he said.

His partner Paix Robinson, who said he was a Welshman by marriage, added that Wales held a special place in their hearts as somewhere they got married and spent holidays, "so it was only right that the first film was in Wales".

Describing the film as a "fantasy that becomes a nightmare", Jones said: "I needed a location that could be beautifully idyllic and hopeful and then turn and become brutally unforgiving".

He added that Anglesey fitted the brief: "It can be absolutely stunning but has a foreboding quality."

A film about tensions arising in the heat of a busy Pakistani takeaway scooped the top honours at this year's film festival.

Luís Hindman received the prize for his film, Magid/Zafar, and was awarded £40,000 to make a new film with an LGBTQ+ theme in the UK.

Hindman said it was "very humbling" to win, and wanted to create something in a British Asian setting that was a "chance to display my mosaic of what British Asianness can look like".

Entertainment.title: Comedian Paul Whitehouse mugged at London cashpoint
Entertainment.text:
Actor and comedian Paul Whitehouse has fought back against someone who tried to steal his card at a London cash machine, according to his wife.

Dr Mine Conkbayir posted on Instagram that her husband had gone out to get some medication on Friday, when he was mugged at a cash machine behind a Sainsbury's in Islington.

"He did fight back and retrieved his card, with the perp scuttling away empty-handed," she wrote, warning people to be "super vigilant" out there.

The Welsh comedian, 68, is known for his work on The Fast Show and BBC's Gone Fishing.

In her post, Conkbayir said Whitehouse was picking up medication for her after she had a bad reaction to some treatment.

"Well, a horrid start to the weekend, would be an understatement," she wrote, adding that she had been encouraged by her husband to make the post "in the hope that it might help folk to be more aware when out and about".

Friends and fans alike have flooded to the comments of Conkbayir's post, condemning the attack and wishing Whitehouse a speedy recovery.

Among them were fellow comedian Dawn French, who wrote that the incident in Islington was "utterly not okay", and Angela Barnes, who said it was a "horrible thing to happen" and she was "sending love to you both".

Whitehouse is best known for his work on Gone Fishing, which he presents alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer.

The BBC Two series began in 2018 and sees Whitehouse and Mortimer discuss life while fishing. It has been nominated six times for a Bafta TV award.

The comedian has also been cast as Hogwarts caretaker Argus Filch in HBO's upcoming Harry Potter television series.

Entertainment.title: BBC pauses civil service secondment scheme
Entertainment.text:
The BBC says it will pause secondments of government statisticians to its fact checking service, BBC Verify, and review their roles.

Since 2018 the BBC has offered six-month secondment opportunities for up to two civil servant statisticians to work for BBC News's head of statistics.

A BBC spokesperson said: "All BBC journalism and editorial decisions are made by BBC journalists and editors, in line with the BBC's editorial guidelines, so the statisticians never make editorial decisions."

Those currently on secondment would not be involved in the publication of news or content during the review and the current round of recruitment will be paused while the role is reviewed, the corporation added.

The decision follows a report in The Telegraph which said embedded civil servants had been engaging in editorial tasks and raised questions about a breach of impartiality rules.

The spokesperson added that the BBC "takes independence and transparency incredibly seriously, and we must ensure we are meeting the highest standards".

They said although statisticians' work had sometimes been recognised with their names on the BBC website, "they never made editorial decisions".

According to The Telegraph, external, a job advert for the 2027 secondment said a successful candidate would have "the ability to influence decision making, working with credibility and proactively with customers to share knowledge and information".

A now-removed blog post written by one civil servant about their placements showed a secondee describing how they had drafted copy for the news website.

Under the scheme, it is understood that statisticians explain data in writing that can be incorporated into stories, but they do not write the copy itself.

Secondees' contributions can be incorporated into journalism that scrutinises the current government, as well as all political parties.

The seconded statisticians also have to adhere to the Civil Service Code of Practice for Statistics. It requires them to present and use data and statistics objectively and not to withhold or misrepresent data due to political or commercial influence.
