Entertainment.title: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake
Entertainment.text:
‘The first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God, this is what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, Mad Men and DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound.

Casual filmgoers may associate Friday the 13th with Jason, the hockey-mask-wearing serial killer. But aficionados will know that Pam, Jason’s mother, is the villain of the first movie. “He didn’t even have the mask until the third movie,” says Cardellini, who has clearly done her homework. “Pam is the original killer, in vengeance of his death.” (There is some massaging of previous storylines in Crystal Lake, such as moving Jason’s drowning from the 1950s to the early 70s, but since the franchise is flexible enough to have sent Jason into space at one point, a bit of timeline tweaking feels fair game.)

The Friday the 13th franchise has a devoted audience – and Crystal Lake’s showrunner, Brad Caleb Kane, is among them. “He’s such a fan,” says Cardellini. “I felt he would have an idea of what fans were wanting.” Kane wrote the part specifically for her, after seeing her in Netflix thriller Dead to Me, which came as a surprise. “My biggest question was, ‘How did I become the person at the front of your mind for this?’” she laughs. Did they feel any pressure in taking Friday the 13th on? “It’s daunting, but hopefully it’s an opportunity to see more of something that didn’t really get its own avenue.”

Anyone who grew up in the 1980s and 90s, as Cardellini did (she is 51), will remember sleepovers with rented VHS tapes and a lot of screaming whenever Freddy Krueger, Michael Myers or Jason Voorhees appeared on screen. “It was forbidden fruit, almost,” she says. “You weren’t supposed to be able to watch it, but you would. And not only the gore but the sexuality – all the things you’re not supposed to be watching. I think it is part of the allure when you’re young. It seems off-limits and rebellious.”

She liked the jump scares and the gore, which is handy, because Crystal Lake is full of them. One vivid sequence involves an astronomical amount of blood. “We reserved a whole week for that,” she says, which is highly unusual for TV, as it tends to move quickly. It had to be precisely planned and choreographed, not least because Cardellini’s hair in the show is lighter, and they soon found that the fake blood stained it pink.

“Even the guy’s face coming off is done on the day with prosthetics, instead of CGI. It’s what you’re actually looking at, which helps with your reaction.” So that wasn’t done in post-production? “No! They pulled it off with fishing wire. So I saw it for the first time as it came off. It stuck with me for a while, because it’s disgusting.” It proved to be one of her highlights. “That’s actually one of my favourite parts of the show. It’s like a blood opera.”

Crystal Lake arrives on a new wave of mainstream horror, from films such as Obsession and Backrooms to Carrie and Widow’s Bay on TV. Why does Cardellini think horror is having a moment? “It’s a great question. I can imagine there’s something about the experience of it that is very present – and it’s a controlled fear, because you know that in a few hours, you will have a resolution. Maybe that is digestible.”

Recently, Cardellini was backstage at a screening of the show at New York Comic Con. “There was some gasping and yelling and cheers – and afterwards, a laugh. That’s when you’re like, ‘OK, this is great, because that’s what the movies did.’ They made you afraid, then you laughed out loud. That is what we were going for. That felt good.”

Cardellini grew up in California and started acting in the mid-1990s. Her breakout was Freaks and Geeks, the Paul Feig/Judd Apatow teen comedy in which she played good girl gone bad Lindsay Weir. The early 80s-set series, a fond, witty look at teenage rebellion, burned bright and fast and was promptly cancelled by NBC in 2000, before its first season had finished airing. As well as Cardellini, it rocket-launched the careers of Seth Rogen, Jason Segel and Busy Philipps.

“If you got cancelled, you were just gone,” she says now. “You didn’t even know where it went. The idea that it would live on, once we weren’t going to make any more, just didn’t seem possible.” Through DVDs and word of mouth, though, Freaks and Geeks slowly became a classic of the high school TV genre. “That it had a life afterwards was a shock – and that it still has a life is amazing.”

On the subject of all-time-greatest TV series, Cardellini joined Mad Men in its sixth season, playing Sylvia Rosen, who has an affair with Don Draper. There was such secrecy around this that when she auditioned, names and details were changed. “I had no idea what I would be doing and [creator] Matt Weiner said, ‘Just trust me, it’s gonna get great.’ I think it was the first two scripts I got – I had one line. I thought, ‘What am I doing? What is this?’” But Weiner had told her it would be a great part and he was not lying. Not only does her character go on to remind Don of a sex worker from his youth, she also gets to leave him, triggering an obsession. “It unfolded like a surprise for me,” she says.

In September, Cardellini won her first Emmy for her role as Carol Love-Smernitch in HBO’s DTF St Louis. “I’ve been nominated before, but winning is a very different feeling,” she says. “It was a wonderful moment.” DTF St Louis is a singular series: Carol is married to American Sign Language interpreter Floyd, but is having an affair with his best friend Clark, a TV weatherman who rides a weird bike and likes to pretend to be a robot during sex. When Cardellini first heard about the show, she thought she knew how the story would go. “A love triangle between a married couple and a best friend, and somebody turns up dead,” she recalls. “But when I read it, I thought, ‘I’ve never read anything like this.’ Every time I thought I knew where it was going, it went somewhere else, in this beautiful, nuanced, very human way.”

The show is a strange, sweet meditation on loneliness, with an offbeat streak. Carol, for instance, is a part-time baseball umpire. “Since I’ve played an umpire, I’ve met so many people who have told me they are also umpires, and it’s people you don’t expect. Also, the parent attacks that they have to weather are pretty funny.” Could she still umpire a game? “Maybe Little League. I don’t know if I can handle the parents!”

That Emmy award now lives on the mantel of her fireplace. Her first appearance on TV was in 1994, when she was a contestant on the quizshow The Price Is Right. You can see it on YouTube – she won a fireplace. Hang on, it’s not the same fireplace is it? “I wish! I don’t have that fireplace any more because, oddly enough, I lost it in a fire.” You lost a fireplace in a fire? “I was working and put a lot of stuff in storage. The storage facility caught fire.” But she had kept it for a long time? “Oh, for years and years and years.”

Earlier this year, Cardellini filmed They Know, a psychological horror movie written and directed by Bill Hader, who also stars. “It’s definitely his incredibly extraordinary point of view,” she says, reluctant to give too much away beyond the fact she plays his ex-wife. The fact that it’s another horror does not mean, however, that Cardellini is in her scream queen era. “I like to change it up,” she says. “I went from DTF to Crystal Lake with one week in between. That seemed like a big left turn. So we’ll see what comes up.” She pauses and adds: “But you never know.”

Entertainment.title: How we made Come Dine With Me: ‘Someone served sushi off a guy’s naked chest!’
Entertainment.text:
Nell Butler, creator

It all started in the early 00s when I tried to throw a dinner party. I was an executive producer during the early days of reality TV – and a house-proud young mum. My posh cousin and her even posher husband came for a meal. I was rushing to get the kids to bed and tidy up, so the food was an afterthought. I’d never made couscous before but decided to serve it with chicken. It was awful. Dry chicken with congealed couscous. At one point, my cousin’s husband stuck his fork in this rock-solid lump, lifted it up and said: “What actually is this?”

When they left, my husband slumped in his chair and said: “I’d give that a three.” I thought there was something funny about scoring somebody’s hosting skills. Everyone leaves those terrible evenings and dissects it with their partner. I came up with the idea of groups of strangers taking it in turns to host, competing for a cash prize.

I pitched it as Ladies Who Lunch, with a Real Housewives vibe. ITV rejected it but Channel 4 daytime were interested. They massively improved it by insisting it should be dinner and everyone had to be a decent cook. The threshold was that contestants had to know what coriander was – that was the test we hit upon. The working title was Let Me Entertain You. Later it became Come Dining, but lawyers worried it was too close to Come Dancing. I suggested Come Dine With Me.

The pilot episode had a narrator who is now a famous actor. He sounded too posh. Replacing him with Dave Lamb’s more casual, sarcastic style took it to another level. The idea of the voiceover talking directly to the contestants was groundbreaking. Dave would throw in “Oh really?” or “God, get a room!”. We’re not there to humiliate or sneer, just to gently take the piss and puncture pomposity, which is a very British trait. Dave walks that tightrope perfectly.

Ratings were pretty good but Channel 4 wavered about recommissioning it. What saved us was that it started doing well on catch-up because students, bless them, alighted on it as hangover viewing. On a Sunday, they’d climb into bed together and watch the omnibus edition. That rescued us. It also gave us traction when selling the format abroad. There are now 50-odd international versions.

It’s a small show that made a big impact. Dinner parties used to be snooty affairs. I hope we helped make them less formal and more fun. I’ve always believed that hosting isn’t to do with wealth, class, the size of your house, or whether you used napkins or paper serviettes. It’s about the warmth of your welcome.

I never imagined Come Dine With Me would run for 21 years. Its staying power is testament to the fact that there’s an endless supply of brilliant ordinary people who make for cracking TV. It’s also cheap to make. We even turned it into a stage musical. I’d like to think we influenced shows like Four in a Bed and Don’t Tell the Bride, maybe even Gogglebox and Love Island’s irreverent narration. And I throw a much better dinner party nowadays. I’ve even nailed couscous.

Dave Lamb, narrator

It started out as a slightly more serious food competition, then they looked at the pilot episode and decided there was more fun to be had by focusing on the people, not the cooking. A few of us comedy performers auditioned to take over the narration. I just improvised around the script. Before long, I was doing lots of asides and mucking about.

“Mango” and “tiramisu” are some of my favourite words to say. I enjoy pronouncing “chorizo” wrongly because it infuriates people. Bruschetta can either be “bru-shetta” or “bru-sketta”, depending on what part of Italy you’re in. Sometimes I’ll do both pronunciations in the same episode, just for mischief. There are filthy bits that don’t make the cut. Occasionally I’ll let go a barrage of truth, shall we say. Obviously that can never see the light of day.

I’m keen for my voice performance not to be unkind. If I wouldn’t say something to their faces, I won’t say it in the voiceover – that’s my yardstick. If contestants are being rude or making fools of themselves, you can see it on screen. It doesn’t need me adding some snide comment.

I realised the show was a hit in 2008 when I was acting in a series called Moving Wallpaper. All these brilliant actors kept saying, “Oh my god, you’re that guy from Come Dine With Me!” I was becoming known as this shouty voiceover bloke. I used to record it sitting down but started losing my voice; a vocal therapist told me I need to stand up because I push it so hard. We do five episodes per session, and by the end I’m spent. My voice only tends to get recognised if I get overexcited. If I get loud and pitch up the register, people go: “You did a bit of it then!”

After this long, it all blurs into one, but certain moments stick in the mind, like sushi being served off a guy’s naked chest. Or the guy who stuck an entire whisk in his mouth. Or the time someone got their pet snake out and it pooed all over the dinner table. One of the most notorious clips is the “What a sad little life, Jane” rant. There’s not much you can add to that, but I was quite pleased with my “Doggy bag, anyone?” line. In terms of horrific dishes, there’s been quite a lot of roadkill.

The longevity of it is bonkers. I assumed it would be one and done. It would’ve been beyond my comprehension that 21 years later, I’d be doing the same job. I think the appeal is about people and their houses. We all have a fascination for where other people live and how they feed themselves. The magic for me is this enormously diverse range of people sitting around the same table.

It’s nicely paid but the beauty of it has been a steady income over a long period. We’re closing in on 2,500 episodes. That’s a lot of shouting! Apparently, humans change all their cells every seven years, so I’ve had three entire bodies while doing this and we’re just about to crack into the next.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have been a deliberate attack.

The independent MP, 65, was struck outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria, on Monday afternoon.

A man, 43, from the nearby town of Tarrawingee was detained at the scene by a passerby and police say a knife was found in the car.

Police are investigating whether it was an "intentional act" but say they do not believe there is an "ongoing threat to the community".

Political leaders have expressed shock and dismay, with Albanese saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy".

While Albanese said it was too early to understand the motive behind what had happened, he did say the political temperature had been rising in Australia.

His Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke backed up that statement with figures showing that reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 in the past year.

Haines was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at 15:35 (04:35 GMT) outside her office on Murphy Street in Wangaratta, police say.

The town, which has a population of around 30,000, is a few hours north-east of Melbourne.

A witness told Australian broadcaster ABC they had heard a bang and seen a woman pinned between two cars, external.

Haines was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta but later moved to Melbourne by helicopter.

After being subdued and detained by the passersby, the suspect was arrested by police.

Announcing that counter terror police were involved in the investigation, the prime minister said: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."

In a statement, Victoria Police said: "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act.

"It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other... The investigation remains ongoing."

An Australian parliamentary report warned last year that threats and physical attacks had increased "significantly over the past decade".

A threat assessment by the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation - the country's equivalent of MI5 in the UK - warned last year that the risk of politically motivated violence was "already flashing red".

Albanese became emotional as he talked about Haines in a live television interview on ABC's 7:30.

He appeared close to tears when asked whether he and his colleagues talked among themselves about the threats and risks they face.

"Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one, one of my colleagues."

He described Haines as having "integrity". In other political reaction:

Opposition leader Angus Taylor - head of the Liberal Party - said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the news, and that Australians would be "angry and appalled by the attack on Helen"

Senator Matt Canavan, leader of The Nationals, said his heart went out to Haines and her family "upon the news of this shocking attack"

Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge said he was "horrified" to hear of the "apparent attack", adding: "Helen is an extraordinary human being and brings people together like few others"

Senator Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader, said violence against elected representatives is "never acceptable". She added: "Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety"

BreakingNewsTab.title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.

In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs."

A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.

The woman is the third complainant the jury have heard from in the trial - and the second to allege rape.

The pair had been attending a birthday party in Soho in London in 2004 when the alleged incidents happened.

She said after the alleged sexual assault, "The visual I remember is just this big grin - it felt like a clown, (with) that sort of weird look in the eye. It was a normal conversation about him being on Big Brother. He just moved towards (me) and grabbed both my boobs".

She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock".

"The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said.

"Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

"I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.

After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."

Russell Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".

Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".

One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".

Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.

One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.

Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.

He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town.

"We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."

Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition.

In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.

Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me".

"Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said before the verdict was announced.

"I still love him and he is still my pastor."

In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder.

"He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing," also speaking before the verdict.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support says court filing
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.

It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.

The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.

The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.

It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.

"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan is scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Researchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees.

The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance.

But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit".

By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said.

Images of the Taraia Object - which Purdue University said was visible in photography dating back to 1938 - led researchers to wonder if it was the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.

"This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years and the mystery continues," said project director Rick Pettigrew, speaking from near the site of the object.

"The island has been holding on to its secrets and it continues to do so. I think eventually someone will find conclusive evidence here," he added.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A space mission is set to launch on Monday that will attempt to grab a piece of Mars' moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth.

If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth.

The spacecraft will blast off from Japan and arrive at Phobos in August 2027.

It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.

Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth.

"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.

There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.

Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.

The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.

It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.

Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon.

"The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained.

"But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."

The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.

Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.

This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.

The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g.

"It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.

"However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said.

Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.

There are two competing ideas.

Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.

Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity.

"When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell.

"It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly."

The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs.

"One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell.

"And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars."

Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists.

The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters.

But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress.

China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031.

We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites.

These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth.

Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water.

Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.

The MMX mission is scheduled to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Center at 04:41 local time on 20 October (20:41BST 19 October).

BreakingNewsTab.title: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.

Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode titled The Revengening, voiced by India-born US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra.

The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret.

Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said.

The character, who has been part of the long-running US animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent.

Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes.

The following year, an episode of the long-running US cartoon addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations, but some viewers found it insufficient.

Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes.

Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise."

Speaking to Variety, external ahead of the weekend's latest episode, Azaria's replacement Malhotra explained: "When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink.

"But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers' room look different now?"

The Grey's Anatomy and The Legend of Korra actor continued: "Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologised for past mistakes?

"Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn't disappoint fans?"

After years of Apu having become a mere background character, Malhotra said he spoke with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos about how they could make the returning fans' favourite more culturally appropriate for 2026.

"It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for long-time fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way."

Apu's wife, Manjula, will now be voiced Janina Gavankar, who previously appeared in Apple TV's The Morning Show and she takes over from Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.

One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.

He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.

The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.

There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."

And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.

It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.

If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine

Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.

"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.

His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.

"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.

He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.

If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.

"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.

Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.

He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.

"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.

"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.

Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.

"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."

But he argued that his team's actions were justified.

"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."

Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."

But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.

Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.

Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.

Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.

Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.

"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.

To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.

Foma has the same rule for his operatives.

"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.

Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.

"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.

So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.

Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.

"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".

But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.

Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.

Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.

"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."

But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.

"Putin won't live forever," he said.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Alberta heads to polls to decide whether to hold vote on separation from Canada
BreakingNewsTab.text:
People in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a binding referendum at a later date on separating from Canada.

The vote was called earlier this year by the leader of the province, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.

Many of those who support separation say the oil-rich province's economic growth has been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.

But those who want Alberta to remain part of Canada - who include Prime Minister Mark Carney - have called for the country to show unity in the face of external pressures.

Polls have suggested that the majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, though the pre-vote debate alone has proven divisive.

Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The province's population is about five million people.

If Albertans do vote on Monday to move ahead with a binding referendum, that could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said.

Smith's decision to allow Monday's vote came in spite of the fact that a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated from Canada.

Following the judge's ruling, First Nations groups have branded Smith's decision to allow the voting process to play out as "undemocratic" and "authoritarian".

Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party of Alberta (UCP), has defended her decision to put the issue to voters. She opposes separation herself, but says the process gives the province's residents a chance to have their say on the issue.

The key question on the voting paper will ask: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"

The separatist movement is led by Mitch Sylvestre, a gun shop owner from the town of Bonnyville, and Jeffrey Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary. They are both members of a group called the Alberta Prosperity Project, which argues that the province's economic growth has been hindered by years of Liberal party rule in Ottawa.

Successive Liberal governments of the last 10 years have put environmental policies above helping Alberta develop its oil and gas sector, they argue. They say Alberta would get to keep more of its wealth if it splits from Canada.

Chris Scott, founder of pro-separatist group Let's Talk Alberta, told BBC News on the eve of the poll that the campaign had already achieved some of its goals, regardless of what happened on Monday. "The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue," he said. "What's started can't be stopped now," he added.

Those who oppose separation say a newly independent Alberta would be left responsible for billions of dollars in debt. They warn that the uncertainty - which they liken to the UK's Brexit vote to leave the European Union in 2016 - would drive thousands of jobs and investment out of the province.

Pro-independence voters told the BBC in Edmonton over the weekend that they feel their voice is not heard in Ottawa, the national capital.

"We really need to send a message to Ottawa, " said Jennifer Trudeau, who calls herself a sovereigntist. She said she did not want a full divorce from Canada, but believes the province needs to "assert its rights".

At a separate unity rally in Edmonton, people told the BBC that they were proud Albertans but felt it was better to keep the country together.

"Alberta is a strong province, but it is important that it stays within a united Canada," said Michele Jackson.

"That is critical to me. I am Canadian 100%."

Micah Sellers called the question about whether the province should pursue independence "ridiculous".

"It's a waste of money," he said. "It's a distraction from real issues in Alberta and in Canada. I think if we're going to be asked, everyone should vote to remain."

Carney has called on voters to deliver a decisive vote against separation. Speaking at a rally on Thursday, he warned that the stakes were high.

"The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," Carney said, echoing warnings he has made in the past about his country's ongoing trade war with the United States.

Alongside the separation question, Albertans will vote on nine other issues - a number of which focus on whether the province should have more control over its immigration system.

Hundreds of thousands of people had voted early by post ahead of Monday, and early figures suggested a strong voter turnout.

The province's election officials will count the ballots by hand, and have 48 hours to complete the task - starting from no earlier than 20:00 local time on Monday (02:00 GMT on Tuesday).

The key question, on separation, will be counted in its entirety first. Officials have said results should be available in the early hours of Tuesday.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.

Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.

Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend.

The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.

His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety.

"It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.

According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.

Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.

Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.

In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"

His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.

In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.

Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics.

"Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.

In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say
BreakingNewsTab.text:
More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.

A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.

The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".

The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".

Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.

At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.

With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.

However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.

The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.

A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.

According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.

The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.

In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

BreakingNewsTab.title: US airman dies as daredevil descent goes wrong before Texas college football game
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A member of the US Air Force died after he fell while abseiling from the ceiling of a Texas stadium ahead of a college football game.

Footage shows the serviceman plummet feet first to the turf midfield at San Antonio's 170ft (52 metre) high Alamodome on Saturday during a ceremony ahead of the game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the Naval Academy.

The airman, identified, external by the military as Sgt Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor at Joint Base San Antonio, died in hospital.

The incident is being investigated. The game between the UTSA Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen continued as planned following the tragic incident.

A collegiate athletic association said the decision to press ahead with the fixture was made before the airman's death had been confirmed.

"We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, teammates and members of the 57th Wing," the American Conference, external said in a statement.

US Air Force Brig Gen Scott Mills said in a statement issued by Nellis Air Force Base: "This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing.

"Tech Sgt Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing."

Patterson, from Fort Stewart, Georgia, had served in the US military for 15 years, according to Nellis Air Force Base.

He held multiple military decorations and was in 2022 named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level.

UTSA president Taylor Eighmy said: "I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member's family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy."

FinanceTab.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
FinanceTab.text:
Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.

The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".

Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.

"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).

Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.

Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.

Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.

"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.

"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."

The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

FinanceTab.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day, says Rightmove
FinanceTab.text:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

One seller - Stewart, from Leicester - said some properties were being filtered out of buyers' search results.

He sold one property, and was now selling his late mother's, and both included an element of leasehold which more buyers have been avoiding. However, he said no one thing defined whether a property would sell at a certain price.

"Part of the issue is trying to work out the right selling price. Properties were on the market high and low but were not selling," he said.

He turned down an offer made on his home a day after it was listed. It was below the asking price and he held out for better offers that never came. In the end, he sold after 18 months for £30,000 less than the original asking price.

Colleen Babcock, of Rightmove, said: "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

FinanceTab.title: Musk and Anthropic pledge share giveaways
FinanceTab.text:
Elon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity.

Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year.

The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn.

The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.

Details over how each American child would be handed a share in SpaceX have not been disclosed.

In a post on social media,, external Musk said: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."

It came after he responded to Anthropic's public fund pledge with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."

Anthropic said none of the shares held in its Public Benefit Fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas.

The Claude developer said on Sunday that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.

In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

FinanceTab.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
FinanceTab.text:
Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned.

Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own.

The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman.

However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

According to the latest figures up to 30 September, external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days.

The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved.

If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate.

Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty".

His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability.

Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim".

He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month".

He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear."

Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death.

On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed.

Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on.

"It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said.

"It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult."

Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings.

However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive.

Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".

Fran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures.

"If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said.

A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off.

"We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays.

"If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses."

A Capita spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the frustration that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme has caused members and their families.

"Our teams are working tirelessly to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

FinanceTab.title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
FinanceTab.text:
Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.

The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.

Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.

There have been laws against playing loud music, as well as singing, on trains since 2005 but the government will remind rail passengers of this with the launch of a national campaign asking people to "share the carriage, not the noise".

The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced.

"We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.

The rail campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages.

Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000.

The government also said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crack down on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.

These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the transport secretary.

Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100.

The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.

Commenting on how fines will be enforced, Chris McDonald, Minister for Science, Research and Innovation, told BBC Breakfast that passengers can complain to staff "or the British Transport Police if they wish".

"They don't have to tackle the individual themselves if they don't feel confident to do that," he said.

Justin from Newcastle-upon-Tyne, welcomed the proposal but wanted to know how it would be enforced.

He told the BBC noise on public transport had stopped him from using buses "due to the levels of antisocial behaviour including this unwanted attendance to someone's social media doom scrolling audio concert".

He said he'd "much rather enjoy my own company with my own music in the isolation of my car".

Transport for London, which operates London Underground, already has by-laws in place to prohibit people playing music or content aloud.

It said that in the first instance enforcement officers will ask the passenger to stop.

"Most people comply at this stage," it said, but added that if someone refuses, they may be asked to leave the train or they could be reported for possible prosecution.

FinanceTab.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
FinanceTab.text:
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".

He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.

A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.

The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.

It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.

There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.

Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.

"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.

"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.

"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."

The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.

The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".

"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.
